abstract.p: Learning from experience to assess threat is crucial for survival and mental health. This function is known to involve several midbrain areas, notably the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey (vlPAG) and dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN). Recently it has been shown that fear learning involves projections from the cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN) to the vlPAG. Here, we show using simultaneous single-unit recordings during fear conditioning that a subset of vlPAG/DRN and FN neurons acquire responses to conditioned cues following learning. Strikingly, these populations exhibit firing covariance and directional functional interactions consistent with their collaboration to the response to cues predicting threat. We also demonstrated the reciprocal monosynaptic connectivity between vlPAG/DRN and FN supporting the interactions between these structures. Together, our findings demonstrate shared dynamical activity within a network integrating midbrain and cerebellar computations during fear learning.

abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: The projections of the cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN) to the midbrain are involved in associative fear learning. Here, we show that during fear learning FN and periaqueductal grey/dorsal raphe (vlPAG/DRN) neurons acquire simultaneously responses to stimuli predicting aversive stimulus. Moreover, neurons encoding such predictive signals in the FN exhibit coordinated activity with the vlPAG/DRN, with directional functional interactions, suggesting that cerebellar – midbrain interactions contribute to the representation of aversive predictions during fear learning. We further characterize monosynaptic projections from the vlPAG/DRN to the contralateral FN, providing an anatomical substrate for reciprocal communications between the cerebellum and midbrain and extending previous descriptions of this pathway.

list-item.p: - Cerebellar fastigial (FN) neurons acquire stimulus specific predictive signals during fear learning.
- FN neurons encoding predictive signals exhibit coordinated activity and directional functional interactions with vlPAG/DRN neurons.
- vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the FN elicit short-latency responses in FN neurons.
- Reciprocal projections link the FN and vlPAG/DRN providing a potential substrate for cerebellar-midbrain interactions during fear learning.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Fear learning is a fundamental adaptive process that enables animals to recognize and respond to life-threatening situations, thereby ensuring survival1,2. Dysfunctions in the mechanisms underlying the acquisition or extinction of fear memories are central to several psychiatric disorders in humans, including post-traumatic stress disorder or generalized anxiety disorder, which severely affect quality of life. Understanding the neural mechanisms that support associative fear learning is therefore essential for advancing our knowledge of emotional processing and mental health. During associative fear learning, a neutral cue becomes predictive of an aversive event after the two have been repeatedly paired. This process, first described by Pavlov3, is driven by prediction error signals (the difference between expected and actual outcomes) which diminish as learning progresses4,5. Neural correlates of this associative process have been identified across multiple brain regions, with activity shifting from the responses to the aversive unconditioned stimulus (US) to the conditioned stimulus (CS) as learning occurs. This transition was initially observed in the lateral amygdala6 and subsequently in other regions such as the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG)7,8, establishing predictive neural signals bound to the CS as a hallmark of associative learning.

Fear learning arises from the coordinated activity of a distributed neuronal network that includes the amygdala, thalamus, hippocampus and prefrontal cortex9,10. The ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG), initially thought as a region only mediating defensive behavior, has since been show to be part of the fear learning network, through its connections with forebrain regions as the amygdala and thalamus, as well as with the cerebellum7,9,11.

Neurons located in the border region of vlPAG and the neighboring dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN) acts as a multifunctional hub during fear learning. This vlPAG/DRN border region thus appears to serve as a multi-functional hub 8,12,13. It mediates behavioral and physiological responses such as freezing10,14 and pain modulation15,16. Neuronal activity in this area reflects threats12,13,17–19 and, during associative fear learning, exhibits a transfer of responses from aversive stimuli to cues predicting the occurrence of these aversive stimuli 7,8. Through connections with the amygdala and other forebrain regions7,20,21, the vlPAG/DRN therefore provides signals that shape the progression of fear learning.

Recent studies have revealed direct projections from the cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN) to the vlPAG/DRN and have demonstrated their influence on aversive learning22–28. Indeed, emerging evidence implicates the cerebellum as a major contributor to emotional regulation and aversive learning29–32. Activity in the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis has been shown to reflect emotional valence and fear-related processes31,33, and cerebellar damage leads to affective instability and impaired behavioral modulation, core features of the cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome34,35. More specifically, inhibition or excitation of the monosynaptic projections from the FN to the vlPAG/DRN has been shown to modulate fear learning23,25. Moreover, stimulation of these projections at the time of prediction error signaling in the vlPAG/DRN was sufficient to alter fear learning, suggesting that these projections contribute to prediction-error signaling in vlPAG/DRN activity7,8,36. Interestingly, a previous report in cats suggested the existence of connections from the vlPAG/DRN back to the contralateral FN37, raising the possibility that reciprocal interactions between the cerebellum and vlPAG/DRN are involved in fear learning.

Reciprocal interactions between structures within the fear network are central to the adaptive encoding of threat. While FN and vlPAG/DRN are interconnected and have been recorded separately during fear learning7,23,25, the coordination of the activity between these regions has not been investigated. In this study, we aimed to characterize bidirectional interactions between the cerebellar fastigial nucleus and the midbrain vlPAG/DRN during fear learning to further understand the mechanisms underlying cerebellar modulation of fear learning. Specifically, we (i) identified neural populations in the FN and vlPAG/DRN that acquired predictive-signal responses to the conditioned stimulus during associative fear learning; (ii) examined the coupling between neural populations encoding predictive signal simultaneously in both structures to study their coordinated contributions to fear learning and (iii) identified and mapped anatomical projections from the vlPAG/DRN to the FN suggesting reciprocal communication between these regions.

sec.title: FN and vlPAG/DRN neural population responses are altered by fear conditioning
sec.p: To characterize neural dynamics encoding fear-stimulus associations in the FN and the vlPAG/DRN border region, we monitored neural activity through simultaneous extracellular recordings from permanently implanted electrodes in both structures in freely moving mice during a CS+/CS- Pavlovian fear conditioning paradigm (Fig.1 a, e). During the fear conditioning paradigm, animals were presented with an equal number of acoustic CS+ and CS- stimuli, consisting of either a 30-second pure tone at 7000Hz or white noise, counterbalanced across animals. The CS+ always co-terminated in a mild aversive foot shock (US), while the CS- was never paired with the US (Fig.1 b). Fear learning success was monitored by measuring the animal’s immobility levels during the CS presentation. Immobility increased from comparable levels during CS+ and CS- presentation during habituation to significantly higher levels during CS+ presentation during recall on the following day (Fig.1 f). However, the relatively high immobility observed in response to CS- suggested the presence of a mild fear generalization. All animals (n=12) were habituated to the acoustic CS+ and CS- stimuli prior to fear conditioning (Fig.1 f).

sec.p: To characterize the simultaneous representation of fear-stimulus associations in the neural dynamics of the vlPAG/DRN and FN, we isolated units from our electrophysiological recordings and compared neural responses following CS onsets and US delivery. To this aim, we defined 5-second reporter time windows (RTWs) at the beginning of the CS and following the US, and compared responses to the first stimulus presentation, before any association has occurred, with the average response across last three presentations, when the association becomes established (Fig.1 c).

We isolated units from the right caudal vlPAG/DRN border region (n=88) and the contralateral medial FN (n=85) (Fig.1 d) using electrode bundles emerging from guide cannulas implanted just above the targeted structures (Fig.1 f).

At a population level, neurons in vlPAG/DRN acquired a significant response to the CS+ onset (RTW CS+ first vs. last 3 vlPAG/DRN: p-value 6.99e-7) whereas no significant modulation was observed at CS- onset (RTW CS- first vs. last 3 vlPAG/DRN: p-value 0.057) following fear conditioning. This suggests that the association between CS+ and US resulted in the acquisition of a response to CS+ broadly in the vlPAG/DRN (Fig.1 g).

In contrast, no significant response at CS+ onset was observed at the population level in FN (RTW CS+ first vs. last 3 FN: p-value 0.181), whereas a significant response to CS- onset was observed (RTW CS- first vs. last 3 FN: p-value 0.006, Fig.1 h). These findings suggest that both FN and vlPAG/DRN adapt their neural activity patterns during fear conditioning, with increased responses to the aversive US and distinct patterns of adaptation to the CS+.

sec.title: CS+ specific predictive signals in FN and vlPAG/DRN subpopulations
sec.p: The analysis above only considered the general behavior of the whole population; however, since the FN and vlPAG/DRN regions may be heterogeneous, we then examined whether subsets of neurons in each region exhibited more specific responses to CS+ onset following fear conditioning. Since the response to CS+ may reflect a change of threat expectation, i.e. increased prediction of an aversive event, we refer to these responses to the CS+ as ‘predictive signals’ (PSs). To identify acquired responses to CS+ onset, we calculated the change in firing rate between the first (naïve) CS+ presentation and the last 3 (trained) CS+ presentations for all units in both FN and vlPAG/DRN (Fig. 2a, c left panel). We then performed k-means clustering on the profile of firing rate changes within the CS+ RTW, and identified groups of units that either exhibited increased responses at CS+ onset (‘PS units’) or did not exhibit such changes (‘non-PS units’) in both the vlPAG/DRN and FN (Fig. 2a, c right panel. PS units, which showed a significant increase in firing rate at CS+ onset relative to their baseline state, were identified in both FN and vlPAG/DRN. Therefore, while FN did not show responses to CS+ at the population level, some units nonetheless exhibited such responses. The increase in firing rate at CS+ onset was significantly larger in PS units than in non-PS units in both the FN and vlPAG/DRN, confirming the relevance of the clustering approach for identifying acquired responses to CS+ in both structures (Fig. 2f, h).

sec.p: To confirm that PS and non-PS clusters represented specific acquisition of CS+ onset responses, we calculated changes in firing rate for all units between naïve and trained CS- presentations (Fig. 2c, d left panel, Fig 2S1). We did not observe a general acquired response to CS-onset in either group, confirming that the PS cluster represents units that specifically acquired a response to CS+ onset in both FN and vlPAG/DRN (Fig. 2c, d right panel). Interestingly, PS units in both the FN and vlPAG/DRN also exhibited a pronounced increase in their response to the US over the course of learning (Fig. 2e, g, f, h). Thus, subgroups of neurons in both FN and vlPAG/DRN acquired a stimulus specific predictive response accompanied by an increased response to the US following fear conditioning.

The PS neurons identified in the vlPAG/DRN are unlikely to mediate a purely aversive stimulus response, as they did not exhibit a strong response to the US prior to fear conditioning (Fig. 2 e). In contrast, non-PS neurons exhibited a clear response to the US prior to fear conditioning, suggesting that this population may include neurons involved in encoding aversive behavior and responses mediated by the vlPAG/DRN.

sec.title: Neural discharge of PS units in the FN and vlPAG/DRN is correlated and suggests bidirectional interactions
sec.p: To examine whether FN and vlPAG/DRN populations exhibit tight temporal functional coordination, we examined the relation between their firing activity before and during fear learning.

We computed cross-correlograms between the spike trains of PS units recorded simultaneously in FN and vlPAG/DRN during the minutes preceding the fear conditioning paradigm and during fear conditioning (Fig.3 a, Fig. 3S1 a, b). Cross-correlograms were always computed with the FN unit as a reference (Fig.3 a). We used the shape of the cross-correlogram to determine the strength and temporal structure of correlations between unit pairs. Many unit pairs exhibited a central peak of a few milliseconds wide, indicating short time-scale coordination of discharge between FN and vlPAG/DRN PS neurons pairs as well as between non-PS neurons pairs already in baseline conditions. Some FN PS neurons also exhibited correlations with vlPAG/DRN non-PS neurons (Fig. 3S1 a). These data indicate that PS-FN neurons are more related functionally to vlPAG/DRN neurons than other FN neurons. Moreover, pairs of PS neurons appeared more likely to exhibit significant coupling than non-PS pairs (Fig. 3S1) suggesting that these neurons may belong to functionally related subnetworks.

sec.p: Moreover, we observed that a number of crosscorrelograms exhibited some degree of asymmetry, with an excess of vlPAG/DRN spikes either following or preceding FN discharge (‘positive’ vs ‘negative’ asymmetry, respectively). To quantify crosscorrelogram asymmetry, we subtracted each crosscorrelogram from its mirror image along the vertical axis. This difference in delayed coincidence between negative and positive time lags was denoted as ΔCC (Fig. 3 a). Pairs with an excess of vlPAG/DRN spikes following FN unit firing (positive ΔCC values for delays in the [3,30) ms interval) were considered as ‘positive asymmetry’ pairs, whereas pairs with an excess of vlPAG/DRN firing preceding FN firing (negative ΔCC values for delays in the [3,30) interval) were considered ‘negative asymmetry’ pairs. Significantly asymmetric pairs were identified both before and during fear conditioning among PS x PS pairs, non-PS x non-PS pairs and PS x non-PS pairs (Fig.3 b-d).

Among positive asymmetry pairs, the cross-correlogram dominantly exhibited central positive peaks, in line with shared inputs and/or excitatory interactions (Fig. 3e). This pattern remained stable under both baseline conditions and fear conditioning (Fig. 3 e,f). In contrast, negative asymmetry pairs rather exhibited cross-correlogram shapes with a central negative peak, more consistent with inhibitory interactions (Fig. 3e). Negative asymmetry pairs in both PS x PS pairs and non-PS x non-PS pairs consistently exhibited negative peaks, whereas FN PS x vlPAG/DRN non-PS pairs showed a mixed pattern (Fig. 3e). Interestingly, this distribution shifted toward negative peaks during fear conditioning (Fig. 3f). These findings suggest that inhibitory coordination patterns may contribute to the adaptation of neural responses to aversive conditions.

Positive asymmetry among PS-PS pairs was preserved between baseline and fear conditioning (Fig. 3g), while both positive and negative asymmetry decreased during fear conditioning in non-PS – non-PS pairs compared with baseline (Fig. 3 h). Interestingly, among FN PS neurons paired with vlPAG/DRN non-PS neurons, both negative and positive asymmetry remained stable from baseline to fear conditioning, while positive asymmetry remained prominent. This suggests that, in PS-PS pairs, the temporal relationship between FN and vlPAG/DRN discharge was maintained, while functional coordination among non-PS pairs decreased during fear conditioning. The preferred temporal order of firing was maintained between FN and vlPAG/DRN PS units, with FN discharge preceding vlPAG/DRN discharge, as well as in pairs in which FN PS units interacted with vlPAG/DRN non-PS neurons. Together, these findings suggest that FN PS neuron discharge are more strongly tuned on vlPAG/DRN activity during fear conditioning and in baseline conditions. They also raise the possibility that vlPAG/DRN non-PS neurons comprise functional subpopulations that become increasingly relevant for learning during fear conditioning, even though they do not initially exhibit the characteristic predictive signal response.

These findings indicate that vlPAG/DRN and FN units participate in shared functional networks exhibiting tight coordination of discharge patterns both before and during fear learning. Moreover, fear learning affects this coordination, notably by weakening the sequential activations of FN and vlPAG/DRN neurons within non-PS populations.

sec.title: vlPAG/DRN units with broader spikes preferentially respond to CS+ after fear conditioning
sec.p: We then aimed to determine whether different neuronal subtypes could be distinguished in vlPAG/DRN based on their waveform characteristics. For each unit, we extracted recovery time, peak to trough width and amplitude ratio (trough-peak/(trough+peak)). We then performed k-means clustering after determining the optimal number of clusters using the silhouette criterion to identify different waveform types (Fig. 3S2 a).

We identified two clusters in vlPAG/DRN, C0 (recovery time 1.705 ± 0.041 ms SEM, spike half width 0.431 ± 0.013 ms SEM, amplitude ratio 0.386 ± 0.016 SEM) and C1 (recovery time 1.535 ± 0.036 ms SEM, spike half width 0.267 ± 0.009 ms SEM, amplitude ratio 0.512 ± 0.0137 SEM) (Fig. 3S2 b). The smaller amplitude ratio and large half width of vlPAG/DRN C0 neurons are consistent with waveform characteristics previously described for putative dopaminergic neurons in the VTA 38. The C0 waveform cluster contained a greater population of PS units in the vlPAG/DRN (n=9/13, Fig. 3S2 c). This distinction was also reflected in the response dynamics of the two populations of neurons, where C0 units developed a strong response to CS+- onset, but not to CS- onset over the course of fear conditioning, while C1 units developed only a weak response to both types of CS (Fig. 3S2 d). Thus, PS and non-PS neurons in the vlPAG/DRN may comprise distinct neuronal populations, with PS neurons being more likely to exhibit broader waveforms in association with the acquisition of a CS+ specific response.

sec.title: Monosynaptic projections from vlPAG/DRN to FN
sec.p: The short-term sequential activations from FN and vlPAG/DRN neurons, evidenced above by ‘positive asymmetry’ in the crosscorrelograms, could involve the excitatory projections from the FN to the vlPAG/DRN area23. To further investigate the anatomical substrates that could underlie the ‘negative asymmetry’ observed in some pairs (i.e. FN neurons preferentially discharging after vlPAG/DRN), we examined whether the vlPAG/DRN reciprocally projects to the FN. To date, such monosynaptic projections from the vlPAG/DRN to the contralateral FN nucleus have only been described in cats37, and we therefore aimed to determine whether they are also present in mice.

To demonstrate the existence of vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the FN, we performed retrograde labelling from the FN by combining unilateral injections of a retrograde AAVretro-mCherry-cre virus in the FN with an injection of a Cre-dependent AAV-pCAG-FLEX-eGFP virus in the contralateral vlPAG/DRN of 5 male C57Bl6N mice (Fig.4 a). This approach revealed distinct labeled somata in the posterior ventrolateral PAG and adjacent lateral DRN with fewer labeled neurons in the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus (LDT), confirming the existence of direct projections from the vlPAG/DRN to the FN (Fig.4 b, d).

sec.title: vlPAG/DRN optogenetic stimulation induces short-latency responses in the FN
sec.p: To assess the effect of direct vlPAG/DRN inputs on FN neuronal discharge, we performed extracellular electrophysiological recordings in the FN in mice expressing channel-rhodopsin-2 (ChR2) specifically in neurons projecting to the FN (Fig. 5S1 a, c) following retrograde rAAV-Chr2-eYFP injections in the FN (Fig. 5 a, 5S1 a). Optogenetic stimulation of these neurons in the vlPAG/DRN via an implanted optic fiber (Fig. 5S1 b) in awake, freely moving mice elicited robust and rapid (<10ms) negative LFP deflections in the FN, with response amplitudes scaling with light intensity (Fig.5 b). Increased firing of FN neurons in response to vlPAG/DRN stimulation (Fig. 5 c, e) was observed in 13 neurons from 3 mice. Response latencies ranged from 15 to 60 ms, consistent with both direct and polysynaptic activation pathways (Fig. 5 b, c). The average modulation of firing rate in responsive units during stimulation also increased with light intensity (Fig. 5 c). These findings indicate that vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the FN can exert a strong and rapid excitatory influence on FN neurons. Together with the anatomical evidence for monosynaptic vlPAG/DRN to FN projections, these results support the existence of a functional circuit linking between vlPAG/DRN and FN neuronal populations.

sec.title: Spatial proximity of vlPAG/DRN to FN and FN to vlPAG/DRN projection neurons suggests reciprocal connections between cerebellum and midbrain
sec.p: We then aimed to characterize the histological relationship between vlPAG/DRN to FN projection neurons and FN to vlPAG/DRN projection neurons to identify anatomical correlates of a reciprocal neural circuit between vlPAG/DRN and FN. Having confirmed the presence of vlPAG/DRN to FN projection neurons, we next examined whether these neurons are anatomically associated with the previously described FN to vlPAG/DRN monosynaptic projections that are functionally important for fear learning23.

To assess potential reciprocal connectivity, we designed a bidirectional transsynaptic viral assay to induce eGFP expression in vlPAG/DRN to FN projection neurons following transsynaptic transfer of Cre recombinase from FN neurons. Specifically, AAV1-pCAG-FLEX-eGFP-WPRE was injected into the vlPAG/DRN and AAV1-mCherry-cre in the FN (Fig. 6 a). Because both vectors possess transsynaptic properties, eGFP expression in vlPAG/DRN neurons should occur when Cre recombinase is transferred across synapses from FN neurons. These experiments may produce FN neurons expressing both mCherry and eGFP (appearing as yellow in merged images). Such co-expression indicates that these FN neurons receive inputs from the vlPAG/DRN neurons (Fig. 6 b left). Conversely, vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the FN and receiving transsynaptic Cre from FN neurons would express eGFP, resulting in eGFP-labeled fibers in the FN (Fig.6 b middle). Finally, the apposition of eGFP labeled fibers to eGFP/mCherry co expressing somata in the FN may provide anatomical evidence for a closed-loop connection between these FN neurons and vlPAG/DRN neurons (Fig.6 b right).

sec.p: We observed co-expression of eGFP and mCherry in both the FN and vlPAG/DRN (Fig. 6 c-e), indicating that Cre was expressed in vlPAG neurons following transsynaptic infection from FN neurons, consistent with the existence of FN neurons projecting to this area. Reciprocally, co-expression was notably observed in large somata in the ventral part of the FN (Fig. 6 f-g), and also in the neighboring vestibular nuclei (Fig. 6 g). In this assay, co-expressing FN neurons receive projections from vlPAG/DRN neurons expressing the FLEX-eGFP vector.

Strikingly, we also observed eGFP labeled fibers in the FN. These fibers may originate from the vlPAG/DRN neurons that received transsynaptic Cre from FN neurons projecting to the vlPAG/DRN. Alternatively, they may originate from another region in which vlPAG/DRN projection neurons and FN projection neurons converge onto a common neuron, allowing for transsynaptic transfer of the viral vector and subsequent labeling of neurons projecting back to the FN. In either case, this these observations are consistent with reciprocal connectivity between FN and vlPAG/DRN projecting neuronal populations. Moreover, we observed close apposition between such eGFP-labeled fibers and FN neurons expressing both eGFP and mCherry (Fig. 6 f, label A (soma) and labels B,C,D (fibers). This spatial proximity is consistent with the possibility that the FN neurons projecting to the vlPAG/DRN and vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the FN form a reciprocal circuit. However, the present anatomical approach does not by itself establish synaptic connectivity or distinguish between direct and indirect interactions.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The neural circuitry underlying fear learning has been extensively described, yet the mechanisms underlying the computation of the prediction error, which drives the learning rate, remain largely unclear. Here, we provide evidence of functional coordination between the FN and vlPAG/DRN neuronal populations encoding the association between the CS+ and the aversive stimulus, reflecting associative fear learning. Moreover, we identified reciprocal projections from vlPAG/DRN to FN, in addition to the previously described FN to vlPAG/DRN projections, suggesting that bidirectional information flow may occur between the cerebellum and midbrain during fear learning and may contribute to predictive signaling. In parallel, both FN and vlPAG/DRN adapted their activity patterns to threat-related stimuli over the course of fear conditioning.

sec.title: Cerebellar inputs shape associative learning via predictive signaling
sec.p: The cerebellum is increasingly recognized as an active contributor to emotional processing 40,41, including the formation and modulation of negative emotional memories42. More recently, the projections of the cerebellum to the vlPAG/DRN border region have been shown to modulate fear learning and extinction23,25. Analysis of the local field potentials evoked by the sound has been interpreted as consistent with an information flow from the FN to the vlPAG, which is inversely correlated with the degree of fear expression43. Consistent with these findings, we observed parallel development of CS+ evoked responses in the FN and vlPAG/DRN following fear conditioning; likely reflecting predictive signals associated with the aversive outcome. Furthermore, crosscorrelograms analysis revealed that, in a subset of neuron pairs, FN activity preceded vlPAG/DRN discharge; suggesting a temporal organization compatible with information transfer from the cerebellum to the midbrain. The origin of the CS+ response in the FN is unlikely to arise from the climbing fiber input from the inferior olive, as described in reward conditioning 44,45. Indeed, such recruitment typically involves complex spikes in Purkinje cells, resulting in transient inhibition of cerebellar nuclei activity, which was not observed in our recordings. While a transient reduction in Purkinje cell firing cannot be excluded, our data do not support a CS+ response driven exclusively by climbing fiber–driven modulation.

sec.title: Direct projections from the vlPAG/DRN to the FN
sec.p: We identified direct anatomical projections from the vlPAG/DRN border region to FN neurons. As previously suggested8,13, this area may operate as an integrated hub recruited during both fear expression and fear learning. This observation is consistent with the established roles of the vlPAG in aversive associative learning7,8 and of the DRN in fear related processes18,19. Serotonergic neurons in the vlPAG/DRN increase their responsiveness to threat during fear conditioning17–19 and can promote behavioral responses appropriate to threat imminence based on their activity patterns46. Here we described a projection from the vlPAG/DRN to the FN. Such projection has been previously reported in the cat37 and its presence in the rodent brain indicates evolutionary conservation of this pathway. We further observed short latency FN responses following stimulation of the vlPAG/DRN projection neurons supporting a functional influence of this pathway. Interestingly, a polysynaptic pathway from the vlPAG to the cerebellar cortex via the inferior olive has also been described 47. However, this pathway has been associated primarily with fear expression rather than fear learning. Anatomically, these FN-projecting vlPAG/DRN neurons identified here appear to be located more ventral and lateral than the vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the central amygdala (CeA), as described by Groessl et al.8. Although their location resembles serotonergic FN projecting neurons reported by Kitzman in 199437, we did not observe serotonin and dopamine reporter labeling in our FN-projecting vlPAG/DRN neurons suggesting that these cells may represent a non-monoaminergic population. We propose that these excitatory projections may be primarily glutamatergic, consistent with the predominance of glutamatergic neurons in the vlPAG23,27, while potentially being modulated by neighboring monoaminergic populations27. The vlPAG also interacts functionally with the cerebellar cortex during fear conditioning47, and several midbrain structures directly project to the cerebellar cortex48.

sec.title: Representation of predictive signal and fear related behavior in the vlPAG/DRN
sec.p: Several neural populations within the vlPAG/DRN contribute to aversive behavior15,27,46,47,49,50, while others have been implicated in predictive signaling7,8,20. Dopaminergic neurons in the vlPAG/DRN have been reported to encode associative strength between CS and US, with their activity shifting toward the CS following conditioning 8,11. Neurons exhibiting predictive signals have also been described as dopaminergic7, which is consistent with the waveform characteristics observed in our PS population. These observations are consistent with the emergence of vlPAG/DRN PS units following fear conditioning. However, in our recordings, vlPAG/DRN PS neurons did not initially exhibit a strong response to the US, which is not consistent with a prediction error signal. We therefore hypothesize that the neurons identified here are not necessarily dopaminergic despite sharing some anatomical and electrophysiological characteristics with dopaminergic neurons. Their location within the vlPAG/DRN also places them in close proximity to serotoninergic populations raising the possibility that they may belong to, or be modulated by, serotoninergic circuits. Still, the absence of a strong initial response to the aversive US in PS neurons suggests that these neurons may not primarily encode the immediate aversive response itself. Instead, their activity may be more closely related to the learned expectation of an aversive event or to motivational processes associated with predictive signaling. Further characterization of their molecular and neurochemical identity will be necessary to distinguish between these possibilities.

sec.title: Cerebellar control over fear related behavior
sec.p: Beyond predictive signaling, vlPAG/DRN neurons may encode a broader threat/fear state involving pain modulation16,51, anxiety related processes mediated by GABAergic interneurons and neuropeptide Y 51 and autonomic responses 52. We hypothesize that some of these functions may represented by the non-PS (nPS) population. Interestingly, we observed stable interactions between FN PS neurons and vlPAG/DRN nPS neurons, suggesting that predictive signals originating in the FN may influence vlPAG/DRN populations that do not themselves exhibit a predictive response. This interpretation is consistent with findings that the cerebellum can bidirectionally modulate fear learning25,53, and suggests that this influence may involve an FN population representing predictive signal. Thus, cerebellar predictive signaling may not only participate in the anticipation of aversive events but may also interact with broader threat-related neuronal populations in the vlPAG/DRN.

sec.title: Identity of neurons participating in the network exchange
sec.p: Several neuronal populations are likely to contribute to the midbrain-cerebellar network described here. Studies in cats have identified vlPAG/DRN to FN projections as serotonergic37, while direct projections from the DRN to the cerebellar cortex have also been reported54. In our recordings, interactions involving FN neurons exhibited both excitatory and inhibitory temporal dynamics, with a predominance of patterns consistent with inhibitory coordination. Several mechanisms could contribute to this organization. First, direct projections from midbrain regions to the cerebellar cortex may influence FN activity indirectly to local cerebellar circuitry. Second, direct vlPAG/DRN projections to the FN may simultaneously influence FN neurons. The excitatory responses observed following optogenetic stimulation of vlPAG/DRN to FN projection neurons are consistent with the clear excitatory influence of this pathway. However, this alone does not explain the inhibitory like dynamics observed in the network-level cross-correlation analysis. One possibility is that vlPAG/DRN projections may engage inhibitory interneurons in the FN55. However, this mechanism would need to be reconciled with the net excitatory responses observed during optogenetic stimulation. Alternatively, the inhibitory like cross-correlation patterns may arise from indirect pathways, convergent inputs, or coordinated activity within broader neuronal network rather that from direct inhibitory synaptic transmission between recorded neuronal populations.

In the network dynamics observed during fear conditioning, FN activity also appeared to precede and coordinate with vlPAG/DRN activity. This observation is consistent with previous descriptions of FN to vlPAG/DRN projections that synapse on glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurons in the vlPAG/DRN27,53. Together, these findings support the existence of reciprocal communication between cerebellar and midbrain populations during fear learning.

sec.title: Circuit dynamics between vlPAG/DRN and FN may support mode switching between baseline and fear states
sec.p: FN and vlPAG/DRN are reciprocally connected, as supported by our anatomical and functional experiments. This organization provides a substrate for reciprocal interactions that could dynamically influence behavior and learning. We observed that, during fear conditioning, interactions involving PS neurons become more prominent relative to the baseline behavioral state. Interestingly, the transition from baseline to fear conditioning appeared to involve broader interactions driven by FN PS neurons more than by the vlPAG/DRN PS neurons, but also with vlPAG/DRN populations that did not exhibit a predictive response. In contrast, interactions involving vlPAG/DRN PS neurons remained more closely associated with PS populations in the FN during both baseline and fear conditioning conditions. These observations suggests that fear conditioning may increase the functional relevance of predictive information within the FN - vlPAG/DRN network. In particular, FN neurons encoding predictive signals may influence a broader group of vlPAG/DRN populations, including neurons that do not themselves exhibit predictive responses. Such interactions could provide a mechanism through which cerebellar predictions are integrated with broader threat-related processes in the midbrain.

Although the anatomical basis for communication between FN and vlPAG/DRN is supported by direct projections in both directions, how these pathways are integrated to generate the functional interactions observed here remains unclear. The circuit is likely to involve multiple synaptic pathways and parallel projections. In addition, neuromodulatory influences, including dopaminergic and serotonergic signaling within the vlPAG/DRN, may contribute to the integration of fear learning and threat related information18,50,56,57.

sec.title: Further deciphering the network between FN and vlPAG/DRN
sec.p: To determine whether and how this network contributes to the transition between baseline behavior and responsiveness to stimuli predicting aversive events, future studies should characterize the molecular and neurochemical identity of vlPAG/DRN neurons projecting to the FN and directly examine their contribution to fear learning and behavior. This would help determine the nature of the information communicated from the midbrain to the cerebellum in an aversive context, and distinguish the contribution of direct midbrain projections to the cerebellar nuclei from that of projections to the cerebellar cortex. For example, projections from the locus coeruleus to the cerebellar vermis59 produce patterns of noradrenaline release resembling the increase in FN firing-rate that we observed during fear conditioning. This raises the possibility that noradrenergic signaling may contribute to the modulation or gating of cerebellar activity during aversive learning59.

sec.title: Implications for maladaptive threat processing
sec.p: In summary, we propose that the cerebellum contributes to associative fear learning by providing predictive signals related to the expectation of aversive events, while its interactions with midbrain structures such as the vlPAG/DRN are recruited during exposure to aversive stimuli. Reciprocal communication between these regions provides a potential substrate for cerebellar - midbrain interactions that are distinct from the inferior olive pathway and may contribute to adaptive fear learning.

This raises the possibility that the vlPAG/DRN–FN circuit could be relevant to disorders involving maladaptive threat processing. Future studies manipulating specific parts of the midbrain-cerebellar circuit will be required to determine whether altering these interactions can modify the anticipation of aversive events and associated behavioral responses, and whether such mechanisms could ultimately have therapeutic relevance.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Adult male C57BL/6N mice (Charles River Laboratories, France) were used for all experiments. Animals were housed in groups of four per cage under controlled environmental conditions (21–22 °C, 40% humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle) with food and water available ad libitum. One week before fear conditioning, animals were individually housed to facilitate handling and behavioral monitoring. Only adult mice aged 8–12 weeks were included in the study. Male and female mice can both be used for fear conditioning studies; however, we used only male mice to minimize potential variability associated with the estrous cycle over the course of our behavioural paradigm. Fluctuations in ovarian hormone levels across the estrous cycle can modulate neural excitability and behavior, particularly in circuits involved in affective and stress-related processing. Estrous stage-dependent changes in neuronal excitability and anxiety-related behavior have been reported in multiple brain regions, including limbic and midbrain circuits, with measurable effects on physiological and behavioral readouts across the cycle 60. The design choice was therefore intended to reduce a potential source of variability within the experimental cohort rather than to imply sex-specific differences in the suitability of the fear-conditioning paradigm. Animal care and experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the European Community Council Directives and applicable institutional and national regulations (authorization number APAFIS#1334-2015070818367911 v3 and APAFIS #29793-202102121752192).

sec.title: Surgeries
sec.p: Surgeries for tracing and electrophysiological experiments were performed in 7–8 weeks-old mice. Animals were placed in a stereotaxic frame (Kopf Instruments) following buprenorphine administration and maintained under isoflurane anesthesia (2%) throughout the whole procedure. Local analgesia was additionally provided by subcutaneously administration of 0.02% lidocaine above the skull. The body temperature was continuously monitored and maintained at 37 °C using a heating pad and a rectal thermometer. For viral injections and electrode implantations, stereotaxic coordinates (in mm) for the FN (AP: −6.43 to 6.49, ML: ±0.77, DV: −2.14 to 2.18) and vlPAG/DRN (AP: −4.45 to 4.49, ML: ±0.55, DV: −2.45 to 2.49) were measured relative to bregma, with the dorsoventral coordinate measured from the brain surface. For viral delivery, a quartz capillary was lowered to a position immediately above the target structure, and 150–250 nl of virus solution was infused. Quartz capillaries (World precision instruments, QTZ,1.0x.50mmx7.5cm, FILMT) were left in place for 5 minutes after the injection before being slowly withdrawn.

sec.title: Histology
sec.p: At the conclusion of the experiments, mice were deeply anesthetized with a mixture of zoletil/xylazine (50 and 10 mg/kg, i.p., respectively) and rapidly transcardially perfused with ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffered SAL (PBS). Brains were dissected and post-fixed overnight at 4 °C in 4% paraformaldehyde, then stored in PBS at 4 °C until sectioning. Brains were sectioned throughout their entire extent at 90 µm using a vibratome (Leica VT 1000 S). Sections were mounted on gelatin-coated slides, dried, and cover slipped with Mowiol (Sigma). Sections were imaged using a confocal microscope (Leica TCS Sp8), and images were processed and analyzed using Image J. Electrode placement and viral injection sites were assessed histologically for all the experiments at the end of the experimental procedures. Animals with no detectable viral expression, or incorrect electrode placement were excluded from the analysis.

sec.title: Fear conditioning and recall
sec.p: For electrophysiological recordings, the following behavioral paradigm was used in freely moving animals. 3 days before to the conditioning paradigm, all animals underwent an assessment of anxiety related behavior. On the first experimental day, animals underwent a CS-habituation session in the morning and fear conditioning in the afternoon. On the second experimental day, animals underwent a recall session.

The CS habituation session consisted in 5 minutes of acclimatization followed by 4 CS- and 4 CS+ presentations, with an inter-trial-interval (ITI) of 20-40 s, and 5 minutes of rest in the experimental chamber. The fear conditioning session consisted of 5 minutes of acclimatization followed by 5 CS+ presentations co-terminating with a foot shock and 5 CS- presentations, delivered in a pseudo-random order with an ITI of 60-120 s and 5 minutes of rest in the experimental chamber. The session always began with a CS+ presentation co-terminating with the foot shock. Recall sessions consisted of 5 minutes of acclimatization followed by 4 CS- and 12 CS+ presentations without US delivery, with an ITI of 20-40 s, and 5 minutes of rest in the experimental chamber.

Two distinct types of CS that were used: 30 s white noise at approximately 65 dB and a 30 s pure tone at 7000Hz and 70 dB. Half of the animals received white noise as the CS+, whereas the other half received the pure tone as the CS+. The US consisted of a 0.5 s, 0.4 mA square wave electrical foot shock delivered through an electrified floor grid at 29.5 s after CS+ onset, such as the shock co-terminated with the CS+. Stimulus presentation was controlled using the Ethovision XT 14 (Noldus).

Fear conditioning and recall were conducted in two distinct contexts (A and B), both located inside of a sound attenuating box (Ugo Basile). CS habituation and fear conditioning were conducted in context A. consisting of a 17 × 17 × 25 cm square chamber with black and white-checkered walls and a grid floor, scented with peppermint-soap. The chamber was cleaned with 70% ethanol between animals. Recall was conducted in context B, consisting of a 17-cm diameter yellow plexiglass cylinder with a grey floor and vanilla odor. This champer was cleaned with 1% acetic acid between animals.

sec.title: Anatomical tracing
sec.p: For exploratory neuroanatomical tracing, a group of mice (n=2) received an injection of 150 nL of pENN.AAV.hSyn.TurboRFP.WPRE.RBG (AAV1, Addgene, 105552-AAV1) in the vlPAG/DRN. For double virus neuroanatomical tracing, an injection of 150-250 nL of pAAV-Ef1a-mCherry-IRES-Cre (AAV Retrograde, Addgene, 55632-AAVrg) into the FN was combined with an injection of 150-250 nL of AAV-pCAG-FLEX-eGFP-WPRE (AAV1, Addgene, 51502-AAV1) into the vlPAG/DRN in male C57Bl6N mice (n = 3). For double virus circuit trans-synaptic labeling, a group of mice received an injection of 150-250 nL of AAV-pCAG-FLEX-eGFP-WPRE (AAV1, Addgene, 51502-AAV1) into the vlPAG/DRN (concentration 10^13), together with an injection of 150-250 nL of AAV1-hSyn-mCherry-P2A-Cre-WPRE (AAV1, Addgene, 107312-AAV1) into the FN.

Mice were deeply anesthetized with zoletil (50 mg kg−1) and xylazine (10 mg kg−1 i.p.), and transcardially perfused with formalin (Sigma) 3–4 weeks after surgery to assess the viral expression. Brains were dissected and post-fixed overnight in formalin at 4 °C and then transferred to PBS until sectioning. Coronal brain sections (50 or 90 μm) were obtained using a vibratome (Leica VT 1000 S), then dried and mounted with Mowiol (Sigma). Sections were analyzed and imaged using a confocal microscope (Leica TCS Sp8).

sec.title: Immunostaining
sec.p: For the immunostaining, 50 µm thick sections containing the vlPAG/DRN were washed with PBS-0.3% Triton X-100. Non-specific binding sites were blocked by incubating the sections for 2 h in PBS containing 3% normal donkey serum (NDS). Sections were then incubated overnight at 4°C in PBS containing 0.3 % Triton X-100 and 1.5% NDS with either a polyclonal rabbit anti-TPH2 antibody (1:400, ThermoFisher PA1778) or a polyclonal guinea pig anti-Tyrosine hydroxylase antibody (1:300, Synaptic systems, 213104). Following primary antibody incubation, sections were rinsed and incubated for 2 h at room temperature with the appropriate secondary antibody: goat anti-rabbit IgG conjugated to Alexa Fluor 594 (1:300, ThermoFisher, A11012) or CyTM3-conjugated donkey anti-guinea pig IgG (1:300, Jackson Immuno Research, 706-165-148). Sections were then mounted with Mowiol and imaged using a confocal microscope (Leica TCS Sp8).

sec.title: Optogenetics and electrophysiological recordings
sec.p: For optical manipulation combined with electrophysiological recordings, mice were injected bilaterally with 200 nL of ssAAV-retro/2-hSyn1-hChR2(H134R)_EYFP-WPRE-hGHp(A) (Zuerich vial facility, v221-retro) in the FN. For optical stimulation, mice were implanted unilaterally with an optic fiber (0.22 numerical aperture, Thorlabs) housed in a stainless steel ferrule (ThorLabs) positioned just dorsal to the vlPAG/DRN. Ferrules were secured to the skull with adhesive, and a protective head cap was constructed using dental cement. Because the vlPAG/DRN preferentially projects to the contra-lateral FN, neuronal activity was recorded in the contralateral FN while the vlPAG/DRN was unilaterally stimulated. To record neuronal activity in the FN, we used bundle of electrodes consisting of nickel/Chrome wire (0.004 inches diameter, Coating 1/4 Hard PAC) folded and twisted into bundles of six electrodes. Pairs of electrode bundles were inserted into metal cannulas (stainless steel, 29 G, 8 mm length, Phymep), to protect the electrodes and ensure accurate placement into the brain. Cannulas and electrode bundles were attached to an electrode interface board (EIB-16; Neuralynx, Bozeman) using Loctite universal glue, in a configuration allowing recordings from the FN. The microwires of each bundle were connected to the EIB using gold pins (Neuralynx). The EIB and all connections were secured in place with dental cement (Super Bond). Electrode impedance was measured at electrodes were gold-plated using a cyanure-free gold solution (Sifco) to achieve an impedance of 200–500 kΩ. During surgery, the electrode bundles were inserted into the brain and the ground was positioned over the cerebellum, between the dura and the skull. Viral injections, optical fiber implantations, and electrodes implantation were performed during the same surgery. Optical stimulation and electrophysiological recordings were performed 3 weeks after surgery to allow sufficient time for ChR2 expression. At the end of the experiments, optic fiber placement, viral expression and electrode insertion sites were histologically verified.

For the optical stimulation intensity ramp, electrophysiological recordings in the FN were performed in freely moving mice placed in an open field arena. Recordings were performed using a 16 channel acquisition system (sampling rate 25 kHz; Tucker-Davis Technology System 3, Tucker-Davis Technologies (TDT)), as previously described61,62. Mice received optical stimulation at 0.5 Hz with a pulse duration of 100 ms. Light intensities of 39.8, 49, 67.8 and 83.3 mW/mm2 at the fiber tip were used. Signals were acquired using a headstage and amplifier from TDT (RZ2, RV2, Tucker-Davis Technologies). Spike sorting was performed with Mountainsort463 (Version: 1.0.4, spike sorting algorithm) in spike interface64 (Version: 0.97.1, python toolkit).

sec.title: Electrode implantation and chronic electrophysiological recordings
sec.p: Extracellular recordings were performed using standard 16 channel electrode interface boards (EIB-16; Neuralynx), to which 2 cannulas were attached, one targeting each recorded region, the vlPAG/DRN and FN. Electrode bundles consisted of nickel chrome wires (16μm diameter, Coating ¼ Hard PAC, KANTHAL Precision Technology) twisted in bundles of 6 wires and gold-plated to achieve an impedance of 200–500 kΩ (cyanure-free gold solution, Sifco). One or two bundles were inserted into each cannula (stainless steel, 30 Gauge, Phymep).

The recording electrodes were progressively lowered until they reached the targeted brain structures, and the electrode interface boards were secured to the skull using dental adhesive resin cement (Super-Bond C&B, Parkell). Miniature stainless-steel screws were implanted on the left parieto-occipital suture, serving as electrical reference and ground. The skin was sutured, and mice were allowed to recover in their home cage for at least 2 weeks. Recordings were performed using a wireless head stage equipped with a battery and connected to a Multi-Channel System W2100 system (sampling frequency: 25000 Hz) using MCS recording software (v1.5.6). Mice were habituated to the head-stage and its weight for 10 minutes per day starting one week before the experiment.

sec.title: Behavioral analysis
sec.p: Immobility was quantified from video recordings acquired using a Basler acA 1300-60gm camera mounted on the same Ugo Basile conditioning behavioral setup and controlled using EthoVision XT 14 software. During electrophysiological recordings, immobility levels during fear conditioning were detected using the video analysis tools in EthoVision XT,. Periods of immobility lasting longer than 2 s during CS presentation were classified as immobility. For contextual immobility levels during habituation and fear conditioning on experimental day 1, the percentage of time spent immobile during the first 5 minutes preceding CS presentation were classified as immobility.

sec.title: Behavioral data statistical analysis
sec.p: To assess group differences between experimental and control animals, an ANOVA was performed to compare immobility percentages during the CS+ presentations during behavior. Analysis was conducted in python using SciPy (Version: 0.13.2) statsmodels (Version: 0.13.2) packages.

sec.title: Electrophysiological signal analysis
sec.p: Electrophysiological recordings were band-pass filtered to retain frequencies between 300 and 8000 Hz and subsequently sorted into single units. Spike sorting was performed using Mountainsort463, with standard settings and a detection threshold of 4 (Version: 1.0.4, spike sorting algorithm) in spike interface64 (Version: 0.97.1, python toolkit). Single units identified by Mountainsort were then filtered according to their firing rate (above 1 and below 150 Hz), waveform characteristics and autocorrelogram shape. Units were retained if their waveform exhibited a trough and a peak separated by a maximum of 2 ms, a maximum halfwidth of 0.6 ms, and a maximum peak/trough ratio of 0.85. Units showing visible noise contamination in their peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) were excluded for subsequent analysis (see Supplementary information). For waveform shape clustering, waveform halfwidth, amplitude ratio and recovery time were computed for each unit. The amplitude ratio was calculated as trough-peak/(trough+peak), while recovery time was defined as the interval from the trough to recovery to baseline. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on these parameters, and the optimal number of clusters was determined using a silhouette test. K-means clustering was then performed using scikit-learn Python package (version 1.7.2.)

sec.title: Optogenetic stimulation coupled with electrophysiological signal analysis
sec.p: To analyze neuronal responses to the optogenetic stimulation, peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs, 1 ms bins) were constructed for each stimulation event. For each stimulation, a baseline window was defined as the 100 ms preceding stimulation onset, and the response window was defined as the 100 ms following stimulation onset. To identify stimulation responsive units, mean firing rate (FR) during the baseline and response windows was compared for each unit using a paired t-test (SciPy version: 0.13.2). To visualize local field potential (LFP) deflections associated with optogenetic stimulation, recordings were butterwoth-band-pass filtered between 0.5 and 300Hz. PSTHs were then constructed around the stimulation onset for each electrode channel and plotted as the mean LFP deflection +/- SEM.

sec.title: Single structure single unit electrophysiological analysis
sec.p: Firing rates were computed from spike-sorted single unit recordings as described above. For analyses performed separately in the vlPAG/DRN and FN analysis windows were centered on CS+ onset, CS- onset or US delivery. For CS onset, the first 5 s following CS onset were analyzed. For US-evoked activity, a 5 s window following US delivery was used, excluding the US itself to avoid stimulation artifacts. These analysis windows are referred to as reporter time windows (RTWs). A 20 s period preceding CS onset were used as the baseline. To visualize population activity during CS and US presentations, peri stimulus time histograms (PSTHs, 1 s bin size), were computed and normalized by subtracting the baseline firing rate. The ‘naïve’ condition was defined as the firing rate of each unit during the first CS+ or CS- presentation or the first US presentation. The ‘trained’ condition was defined as the mean firing rate across the three last presentations of the corresponding stimulus (the 3rd,4th and 5th presentations).

For naïve versus trained comparisons, the mean firing rate within each reporter time window (RTW) was calculated for each unit after subtraction of the baseline firing rate. Naïve and trained responses were then compared using Wilcoxon-rank test (R stats package version 4.1.2). The change in firing rate (Delta FR) was computed for each unit by subtracting the naïve response from the trained response. To classify units as PS and non-PS units, k-means clustering was performed on the Delta FR values calculated within the 2 to 6 seconds window following CS onset. Differences in responses between PS and non-PS units during CS+ or CS- presentations or following US delivery were assessed using the mean FR within the corresponding reporter time windows (RTW) and the Wilcoxon rank test. The analysis were performed in R (version 4.1.2 (2021-11-01)) using Rstudio (2023.12.1.402).

sec.title: Connectivity analysis
sec.p: Cross-correlograms were computed between simultaneously recorded units from different structures within the same animal according to their cluster affiliation. Correlograms were calculated for PS – PS pairs, non-PS – non-PS pairs and PS – non-PS pairs. Spike-trains were analysed during 2 time windows: baseline, define as the 5 minutes preceding the first CS presentation and fear conditioning, emcompassing the period from the first to last CS presentation. Cross-correlograms were computed using 3 ms bins over a window of 300 ms. Cross-correlograms were then summarized in a matrices according to neuronal pairs type and behavioral condition. Asymmetry was quantified by comparing the number of spikes in the 27 ms preceding and following the reference unit discharge. The statistical significance of asymmetry was assessed using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero. Significant pairs were classified according to the direction of asymmetry: positive asymmetry was interpreted as the vlPAG/DRN unit preferentially firing after the FN reference unit, and negative asymmetry as the vlPAG/DRN unit preferentially firing before the FN reference unit.

For the analysis of changes in asymmetry across behavioral conditions, mean asymmetry values for each neuronal pair subgroup were compared between baseline and fear conditioning using ANOVA over the 15-ms period following reference unit discharge. For comparisons of asymmetry between neuronal subgroups within the same time window, group-averaged cross-correlograms were visualized over a 20-ms window before and after reference unit discharge using 5-ms bins. Statistical comparisons were performed on the summed asymmetry values across the first three 3-ms bins (9 ms in total) following reference unit discharge using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Statistical analyses were performed in R using the stats package (version 4.1.2).

sec.title: Sample sizes and statistical tests
sec.p: For the electrophysiological analysis, sample sizes were determined by the number of neurons reliably recorded from the experimental animals and were comparable to those used in previous in vivo electrophysiological studies24,53. Given the relatively small sample sizes and the paired nature of the observations, differences between time points were assessed using the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which does not require the assumption of normally distributed data. For the asymmetry analyses, statistical significance was similarly assessed using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test against zero. For group comparisons, repeated-measures ANOVAs were used to assess the effect of condition over time. The same animals were repeatedly assessed across different conditions and/or time points, allowing within-subject changes and condition-by-time interactions to be evaluated while accounting for the paired nature of the observations. For anatomical studies, sample sized were determined based on the number of successful tracings and staining experiments and were comparable to those reported in previous studies24,53.

body.p: This valuable study combines simultaneous recordings, viral tracing, and optogenetics to show coordinated activity and reciprocal connectivity between the cerebellar fastigial nucleus and the periaqueductal gray/dorsal raphe during fear learning in mice. The evidence that this coordinated activity reflects threat prediction is incomplete because of modest behavioral discrimination, a focus on a small subset of neurons despite population responses favoring the non-predictive cue, limited statistical support for the cross-correlations, and under-quantified anatomy. The work will be of interest to researchers studying cerebellar and midbrain contributions to fear.
Summary:

In this manuscript, Urrutia Desmaison and colleagues perform dual-site in vivo electrophysiological recordings from the fastigial cerebellar nucleus (FN) and the midbrain ventrolateral periaqueductal gray/dorsal raphe nucleus (vlPAG/DRN). Numerous studies have demonstrated that the FN projects to the vlPAG/DRN, but no studies have examined the functional relationship of these brain populations during fear learning. The authors demonstrate that neurons in both the FN and vlPAG/DRN can acquire responses to the conditioned stimulus presentation, suggesting their participation in fear learning. They further show that these neurons are functionally coupled with one another using cross-correlation analysis. Finally, they demonstrate that in addition to FN->vlPAG projections, there is also a vlPAG->FN projection, which is likely glutamatergic. This creates a potential closed cerebellar loop, through which cerebellar learning may contribute to fear learning paradigms.
Strengths:

The data presented are the first simultaneous neural recordings from the fastigial nucleus and the vlPAG during fear learning and recall. These recordings permit analysis of coordinated activity across brain regions, as well as an assessment of how neural populations in each region shift during learning. This work, therefore, makes critical advances in our understanding of how the cerebellum contributes to fear learning, an emerging area of interest in the non-motor roles of the cerebellum.
Weaknesses:

While the data presented is novel, I have a number of major concerns that detract from the overall strength of the paper. One of my biggest concerns is that the authors focus extensively on a CS+ predictive signal neuron in the FN, despite the observation, at the population level, that the majority of FN neurons respond to CS- trials. Whether and how these populations correlate with vlPAG/DRN activity is not discussed. Additionally, there is a general lack of statistical analysis presented throughout the manuscript, making it difficult to ascertain the veracity of the claims being made. The anatomical data presented are also under-analyzed, making conclusions on the nature and strength of the bidirectional connectivity difficult to ascertain. Finally, at a more fundamental level, the mice did not seem to acquire strong, specific fear conditioning, making interpretation of the underlying neural responses somewhat difficult to assess.
Major Concerns:

(1) Numerous citations are incorrect throughout the manuscript. These need to be corrected to properly attribute prior work. Please read through the references carefully to ensure that all citations are correct.
(2) A major limitation that only male subjects were used - estrous cycle variability aside the study would be stronger to include both male and female subjects.

(3) Can the authors comment more on the inclusion/exclusion criteria for neural recording placement? The images in Figure 1 show a relatively wide variation in rostral-caudal targeting in both the vlPAG/DRN and in the FN. Was there any systematic correlation between neural response properties and recording location? The electrode track in the FN (Figure 1e) does not appear to be fully within the FN - what was the total distance of the electrode contacts from the tip of the electrode? Also, please include scale bars on Figure 1e.

(4) I am concerned with the high immobility the animals demonstrate during the CS- condition. Immobility increased from ~30% in the habituation trials to 60% in the recall trials for the CS- trials - a near doubling of the immobility, suggesting more than a 'mild fear generalization'. Additionally, the fear separation in immobility during the fear conditioning phase does not clearly separate between the CS+ and CS- until the very last trial. This data suggests that the animals did not adequately differentiate the CS- and CS+ conditions, which therefore makes claims related to neural transfer during learning difficult to reconcile.

(5) The authors compare the response during the first trial RTW with the average of the last 3 RTW. Given that the behavioral responses between CS- and CS+ were statistically indistinguishable on trial 3 and trial 4 - this comparison seems problematic. Why not compare the response on trial 1 with the response on trial 5, in which there is clearer separation between the CS+ and CS- conditions?

(6) The authors stratify their recordings by neurons that respond to the CS+ onset RTW, which they refer to as PS (predictive signals) neurons. However, at the population level, FN neurons showed a preferential response to the CS- trials. They observe a proportion of cells in both the FN and vlPAG/DRN that are responsive to CS+ onset. The authors should specifically state what proportion of cells in the FN and vlPAG/DRN are classified as CS+ PS neurons (in later experiments, it seems ~13 cells in the vlPAG/DRN, unknown how many in the FN). It is also not clear what the criteria were for categorization of CS+ responsive vs. non-responsive. Since the FN population responded most strongly to CS- onset, the authors should do a similar analysis and cellular stratification with CS- trials. They seem to demonstrate that neurons that responded to the CS+ (i.e. the CS+ PS neurons) did not acquire responses to the CS-; however, in the FN there must be a separate population of CS- responsive neurons that contributes to the increase in population responses during the CS- presentation.

(7) The authors should comment on the US response of both PS and non-PS neuron populations in the fastigial nucleus; these responses likely represent sensory responses, and are not concerning in and of themselves, but they should be mentioned and discussed explicitly.
(8) It is not clear what is being plotted in Figure 2f/h bottom panels. It is not discussed in the text, and the figure legends do not clearly describe these panels.

(9) The cross-correlation data is very difficult to follow in the text and figures. I would recommend splitting the data into pair types (PS-PS; PS - nPS; nPS-nPS) and including only the first pair type in the main text/figure, with the other correlation patterns shown in figure supplements. Alternatively, if they deserve more prominent space than a figure supplement, multiple smaller figures may be better suited to maintain clarity.

(10) The observation that most of the CS+ PS neurons were C0 phenotype (broader spike) is interesting given work in the field on vlPAG/DRN prediction error signaling (Walker et al., 2019) and the potential role of vlPAG/DRN dopamine neurons in this process (Groessl et al., 2018). Were the FN CS+ PS neurons preferentially coupled to C0 neurons? If so, this is interesting given the known anatomical connection between FN and vlPAG/DRN dopaminergic neurons (Vaaga et al., 2020) and should be discussed more fully and reconciled with existing literature. Is it possible for the authors to separately analyze the FN correlation with C0 and C1 neurons?
(11) The reciprocal anatomical data shown is under-analyzed. Additional analysis and quantification of the number of cells labeled, as well as appositions, should be provided.

(12) The conclusions in the discussion are not fully supported by the data; the CS+ FN neuron population seems small, and at a population level, FN responds more to the CS- than CS+. Further experiments would need to clarify whether and how disrupting cerebellar input to the vlPAG/DRN specifically disrupts predictive error signaling - which is not done in this manuscript.
Summary:

This research builds on previous findings that cerebellar- periaqueductal grey projections contribute towards fear acquisition. The study reports three novel primary findings. Firstly, the authors show that a subset of neurons in both the cerebellar medial nuclei and vlPAG/DRN can independently signal the acquisition of auditory cued aversive stimuli by increasing their responsiveness to the CS+ signal. This has not previously been reported in the FN and is supportive of prior findings in relation to the vlPAG/DRN. Secondly, they demonstrate cross-correlational activity between different subgroups of neurons in each of these regions. This is supportive of previous research demonstrating FN modulation of vlPAG, but goes further to demonstrate a possible modulation in the reciprocal direction. Lastly, using anatomical tracing and optogenetics, the authors demonstrate a feedback loop from the vlPAG/DRN to the FN to support the evidence of bidirectional connectivity. The optogenetics study provides the most robust functional evidence of this and is supported by anatomical tracing. These findings provide a significant step in understanding cerebellar output in relation to conditioned defensive states and cerebellar-midbrain related feedback loops. The results provide a useful basis for further investigation of the role of this reciprocal connectivity and processing of aversive cues.
Strengths:

We commend the authors on collecting data from such technically challenging experiments. Recording simultaneously from two brain regions (especially the cerebellar nuclei) and maintaining stability during fear conditioning is difficult. By identifying a subset of CS+ neural responders during acquisition, this methodology has allowed the authors to demonstrate how activity in the cerebellar nuclei is updated during cued fear learning and its contributions to predictive signals in general. The experiments address a highly topical and interesting question about reciprocal loops between midbrain regions and the cerebellum, providing evidence from cross-correlograms, optogenetics and viral tracing strategies. The optogenetics experiment provides the most robust proof of monosynaptic and multisynaptic projections from the vlPAG/DRN to the FN. The study also highlights an interesting way to investigate this question using AAV1 serotype viral vectors, and although this method has its limitations, they are well addressed in the discussion.
Weaknesses:

(1) The authors have identified neurons as originating in vlPAG/DRN regions as this is more accurate than identifying recordings from vlPAG regions only. The findings should be interpreted in light of possible differences along the dorsoventral and rostrocaudal axes, as the PAG is known to show somatotopic and functional organisation along both axes. Such differences may be reflected in response profiles or anatomical connectivity.

(2) Unsupervised clustering of units can sometimes mask heterogeneous findings; for example, the average looks flat, but on an individual level there might be units that are excited, suppressed, or unresponsive. Findings from the cluster analysis were based on a 5-second reporter window that might not capture some of the finer-grained temporal dynamics that occur with onset of fear acquisition of the CS+. It might, for example, include motor-related activity that hasn't been controlled for. The cluster analysis only identified two groups of units that either increased firing or were non-responsive. This should be interpreted with care, as within a population you might expect to see neurons that reduce activity, or subtle groupings related to response latencies that only contain a few cells but have been masked by this type of analysis.

(3) The results and discussion do not fully explore/account for why, in Figure 1g and h, for the FN there is an increase in responsiveness to the CS- (an innocuous tone over time), while there is no such observable increase in the group data during conditioning with the CS+. In the supplementary Figures 2 C, D and F, there doesn't appear to be a population of units that accounts for this increase in responsiveness to the CS-.

(4) An important next step would be to investigate more directly the functional role of the reciprocal projection from vlPAG/DRN to FN in the context of fear learning. It remains unclear whether this pathway is functionally involved in modulating activity in the FN in relation to fear acquisition, but also other aspects of the fear conditioning process, such as maintenance of the fear memory and extinction.
